figures.shows: (a) Effective refractive index (y, about 1.57 to 1.66) against waveguide top width (x, about 520 to 660 nm) for the 775 nm TM2 mode (red, steep rise) and the 1550 nm TM0 mode (black, gentle rise); the curves cross at about 590 nm and an index of about 1.607. Insets: two mode profiles and a cross-section schematic (LN on SiO2 on silicon). (b) SEM of a microring (scale bar 80 µm). (c) SEM of a waveguide array (scale bar 50 µm). (d) SEM of a waveguide cross-section (scale bar 500 nm).
figures.confirmed_by: natural phase matching between 1550-nm TM0 and 775-nm TM2 modes can be obtained by varying the top width of the LN waveguide around 590 nm

figures.shows: Schematic of SHG in a waveguide and a microring on a Z-cut chip, with a pump input, a cavity build-up label and a '~10 X Enhancement' label. Inset left: mode overlap between the 1550 nm TM0 and 775 nm TM2 profiles. Inset right: energy scheme of the nonlinear conversion (ω1, ω2, ω3).
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 2: Schematic of second harmonic generation in a waveguide and microring resonator.

figures.shows: (a) Normalized SH power (y, 0 to 1, arbitrary units) against pump wavelength (x, about 1530 to 1566 nm) for the 1 mm waveguide: measured points and fitted curve. (b) SFG signal output (y, mV, about 95 to 100) against time (x, ns, 524.2 to 525.2): baseline about 98.7 mV, dip to about 96.7 mV at about 524.7 ns, measured points and fit.

figures.shows: Generated SH power (y, nW, 0 to 160) against input pump power (x, mW, 0 to 35) for the 1 mm waveguide (red diamonds, fitted curve) and the 80 µm radius microring (black squares, fitted curve). Both rise quadratically. The microring reaches about 150 nW at about 26 mW pump, and the waveguide about 18 nW at about 32 mW. Inset: photograph of the microring lit by SH light.

figures.shows: Experimental setup for the signal-depletion measurement: two synchronized optical channels (tunable laser TLS, EOMs, pulse generator, AWG, FPCs), a pre-amp, OTF and EDFA on the pump channel, a DWDM combiner, the device under test (microring and nanowire), a photodiode with OTF and an oscilloscope on a synchronizing clock.
figures.confirmed_by: S. 1. Experimental setup with two synchronized optical channels.

figures.shows: Normalized SH power (y, 0 to 1) against pump wavelength (x, 1530 to 1570 nm) for the L = 1 mm waveguide at 28.5 °C: measured points and fit for 594 nm top width, and simulated curves for 588, 590 and 592 nm top widths. The simulated sections reproduce the main peak at about 1548 nm and the side peaks at about 1543 nm and about 1552 nm.
figures.confirmed_by: we observe multiple side peaks along with a central phase matching peak on this 1-mm long waveguide.

figures.shows: (a) Simulated effective index (y, about 1.606 to 1.6075) against wavelength (x, 1549 to 1555 nm) for 1550 nm TM0 (solid) and 775 nm TM2 (dashed) at temperatures 24.5 to 64.5 °C in 10 °C steps. Crossing points move to longer wavelength with temperature. (b) Measured normalized SH power against wavelength (x, about 1545 to 1553 nm) at 28.5 °C (red) and 48.5 °C (green). papers.what_it_is: An experimental and simulation paper on modal phase matching for second-harmonic generation in Z-cut lithium-niobate-on-insulator waveguides and microrings, with a supplement on setup, a model and thermal tuning.
papers.why_not: The paper is about integrated nonlinear photonics (SHG in LN waveguides and microrings). It has no machine-learning, finance or statistics workload. It only mentions quantum information applications as motivation. The new assertions are tagged 'qc' as the nearest context.

assertions.value: The authors report a normalized SHG efficiency of 26%W−1cm−2 in a 1 mm long Z-cut LNOI waveguide, derived from a 2% signal depletion in an SFG measurement with 7.7 W peak pump power on chip.
quotes: we observe a clear 2% dip (ηdip, averaged over 50 million
measurements) on the signal with 7.7-watt pump peak power on chip
which is 2.3 times less than the predicted value of 61%W −1cm−2
we observe a 26% W −1cm−2 normalized
assertions.certainty_reason: Single-device measurement by the authors.
assertions.reader_inference: The 26%W−1cm−2 figure comes from an SFG depletion measurement used to validate the SHG efficiency, not from a direct SH-power calibration.

assertions.value: The authors state a theoretical normalized efficiency of approximately 61%W−1cm−2 for a perfectly phase-matched (ΔK = 0) LN waveguide, which is 2.3 times above the measured 26%W−1cm−2.
quotes: The theoretical normalized eﬃciency is calculated to be approximately 61%W −1cm−2
which is 2.3 times less than the predicted value of 61%W −1cm−2
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation result stated by the authors; the Eq. 1 integral is not reproduced in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors attribute the gap between the measured and predicted efficiency, and the non-ideal phase matching curve, to LN film inhomogeneity and fabrication errors accumulated over the 1 mm waveguide.
quotes: is likely caused
by the LN thin ﬁlm inhomogeneity and fabrication errors accumulated over the 1 mm waveg-
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as a likely cause; not isolated by experiment.

assertions.value: The authors simulate that natural phase matching between the 1550 nm TM0 and 775 nm TM2 modes is obtained near a waveguide top width of 590 nm, for a 70° sidewall angle.
quotes: natural phase matching between 1550-nm TM0 and 775-nm TM2 modes can be obtained by varying the top width of the LN waveguide around 590 nm
assertions.certainty_reason: FEM simulation result stated by the authors.

assertions.value: The authors state that Z-cut LNOI wafers give access to the d33 tensor element in all propagation directions in quasi-TM modes, so phase matching can be kept on the entire X-Y plane, whereas phase matching between quasi-TE modes on X-cut wafers is restricted to propagation along the Y-axis.
quotes: Z-cut LNOI wafers provide access to the d33 tensor in all propagation directions of light in quasi-TM modes
the propagation direction of the interacting lightwaves is restricted to only along the Y-axis
assertions.certainty_reason: Design rationale stated by the authors; no propagation-direction dependence was measured in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper tests only straight waveguides and microrings; it does not measure phase matching versus propagation direction.

assertions.value: The authors state that the birefringent quasi-TE/quasi-TM phase matching approach works through the d31 and d32 tensor elements, whose nonlinear coefficients are 4 to 5 times lower than d33.
quotes: 4 to 5 times lower than d33.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without a citation in the passage.

assertions.value: The authors state that the index contrast of about 0.6 between LN and the silica cladding gives negligible bending loss for radii down to 15 µm.
quotes: is about 0.6, which gives rise to negligible bending loss even for small radii down to 15 µm
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated by the authors without a bending-loss measurement in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors report that the devices are fabricated on a 400 nm thick LN film on a 2 µm silica layer, with electron-beam lithography, ion milling and a 2 µm PECVD silica over-cladding. The etched sidewall angle is 67° ± 3°.
quotes: which is a 400 nm thick LN thin
an optimum sidewall angle (67◦ ± 3◦)
a layer of 2 µm thick silicon dioxide is deposited via plasma enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) as over-cladding
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own description of its device setup.

assertions.value: The authors report that the LN layer is non-uniform by ± 20 nm across the wafer and that accumulated fabrication errors are ± 30 nm. They define waveguides with widths from 500 nm to 700 nm in 2 nm steps to find the optimum phase matching.
quotes: non-uniformity (± 20 nm) of the LN layer across the whole wafer
accumulation of fabricate errors (± 30 nm)
waveguides with various width ranging from 500 nm to 700 nm with 2 nm step size
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state these fabrication tolerances as limits on achieving phase matching.

assertions.value: The authors report a fiber-to-waveguide coupling efficiency of about 15% at the pump wavelength and a SH output coupling efficiency of at most 10%. They note that estimating the SH output coupling is difficult.
quotes: (coupling eﬃciency ≈ 15%)
However, the coupling eﬃciency for the SH light is quite low (≤ 10%)
curate estimation of the output coupling eﬃciency for the SH light is diﬃcult
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the coupling limitation on their SH-power measurement and use SFG depletion to validate the efficiency.

assertions.value: The authors state that signal depletion in sum-frequency generation is a more accurate way to determine the conversion efficiency than SH power, because it needs only the IR TM0 coupling efficiency.
quotes: The signal depletion
measurement is more accurate in determining the nonlinear conversion eﬃciency
assertions.certainty_reason: Methodological claim by the authors.

assertions.value: The authors report that the SFG pump is a 10-MHz pulse train with 130-ps FWHM, and that the quasi-CW signal has about 10 ns FWHM and is temporally aligned with the pump.
quotes: 10-MHz pulse train with 130-ps full width at half maximum (FWHM)
The quasi-CW signal with wider pulse width (∼ 10 ns FWHM) is synchronized and temporally aligned
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own description of its measurement setup.

assertions.value: The authors report a measured bandwidth of the central SHG phase-matching peak of about 1.9 nm in a 1-mm waveguide, against a simulated bandwidth of 0.9 nm. They attribute the difference to film thickness variation, compositional inhomogeneity and fabrication errors.
quotes: bandwidth of the central peak in terms of the pump wavelength is measured to be about
1.9 nm. However, our simulation based on the measured waveguide cross-section predicts
a 0.9 nm bandwidth.
we observe multiple side peaks in addition to a central phase matching peak for a 1-mm long waveguide
assertions.certainty_reason: Single-device measurement compared with simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report an empirical model that treats the 1 mm waveguide as 3 sections of shorter waveguide with different top widths (588 nm, 590 nm and 592 nm plotted). It reproduces the secondary phase-matching peaks seen in the measurement.
quotes: by decomposing it as 3 sections of shorter waveguide with
top width of 588 nm, 590 nm. 592 nm are plotted in S. 2.
thus causing the presence secondary phase matching peaks that matches experimental observation.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical model for one device; the section widths are not independently measured.
assertions.reader_inference: The model is a qualitative explanation of the side peaks, not an independent measurement of the width variation.

assertions.value: The authors report that the waveguide phase-matching wavelength shifts by +0.065 nm per 1 °C, measured as a 0.13 nm red shift for a 20 °C increase. The simulation gives 0.062 nm/°C, and they conclude the thermo-optic effect dominates.
quotes: shift by +0.065 nm per 1◦C increase
at the rate of 0.062 nm/◦C
primary phase matching peak is red shifted by 0.13 nm with temperature increased by 20 ◦C, which is corresponding to 0.065 nm/◦C.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single-device measurement with agreeing simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report microrings with top widths between 575 and 625 nm and radii around 80 µm. They use the large radius to obtain a small free spectral range and improve the chance of natural phase matching between resonances near 1550 nm and 775 nm.
quotes: We next fabricate LNOI microrings with top width varied between 575 and 625 nm.
we make a series of microrings with large radii around 80 µm
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own description of its device design.

assertions.value: The authors report measured FSRs of 2.0 nm (quasi-TM) and 2.2 nm (quasi-TE) for the 80 µm microring. The text gives loaded Q factors of 4×10^4 and 1×10^4 in that order, and the authors say sidewall roughness largely limits Q.
quotes: the FSR of the quasi-TM and quasi-TE modes are measured to be 2.0 and 2.2 nm, respectively, with the loaded cavity quality factors of 4 × 104 and 1 × 104.
the quality factor for the current microrings is largely limited by the sidewall roughness.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single measurement; the text is internally inconsistent about which mode has which Q.
assertions.reader_inference: Figure 4(a) labels TM0 as Qload ≈ 10^4 and TE0 as 4×10^4. That is the reverse of the text's order, but matches the text's statement that TE modes have higher Q. The text also says TM modes are more widely spaced than TE, yet gives 2.0 nm (TM) and 2.2 nm (TE), and gives a TM FSR of about 2.3 nm earlier on p.9.

assertions.value: The authors state that the thermo-optic difference Δd is relatively small for these devices, so the resonance misalignment that thermal tuning can compensate is fairly limited. They use large rings with many resonances so that some resonance fits within the tuning range.
quotes: small so that the amount of resonances misalignment that can be compensated is fairly limited.
we use large microrings to increase the number of resonant modes
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of thermal tuning for their devices.

assertions.value: The authors report simulated cavity thermo-optic coefficients of 0.0193 nm/°C (1550 nm TM0) and 0.0167 nm/°C (775 nm TM2), giving Δd = -0.0141 nm/°C, and an estimated ΔT of 11.0 °C.
quotes: cavity modes to be 0.0193 nm/◦C and 0.0167 nm/◦C, respectively.
we estimate that ∆T = 11.0 ◦C
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation-derived values using a generalized Sellmeier equation.

assertions.value: The authors report that the FWHM of the fitted Lorentzian temperature-tuning curves for three resonances on the same chip is 12.5 ± 1.5 °C, in agreement with the theoretical value of 11.0 °C.
quotes: are 12.5 ± 1.5 ◦C, which agrees with the theoretical value of
11.0 ◦C (see supplementary for details).
assertions.certainty_reason: Three resonances on one chip.

assertions.value: The authors report that the out-coupled SH power from the 80 µm microring is 10 times higher than from the 1 mm straight waveguide at the same pump power, while the cavity is under-coupled for the SH TM2 mode. Both devices show a quadratic dependence on pump power, with fitted powers of 1.95 and 1.88.
quotes: the out-coupled SH power from the microring is 10 times higher than the straight waveguide
polynomial power of 1.95 and 1.88, respectively
assertions.certainty_reason: One waveguide and one microring compared.
assertions.reader_inference: The 1.95 and 1.88 fits and the authors' statement that this indicates undepleted-pump SHG support the comparison being made in the low-power regime.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 5: at about 26 mW input pump the microring SH power is about 150 nW, and at about 32 mW the waveguide SH power is about 18 nW. At about 25 mW the waveguide is at about 11 nW.
quotes: Figure 5: Comparison of second harmonic generation between a straight waveguide and a microring resonator of similar cross-section geometry.
assertions.certainty_reason: Values read by eye from the plot.
assertions.reader_inference: These read-off values give a ratio of roughly 10 or more at equal pump, in line with the stated 10 times.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 4(b): the SH-power versus temperature curves for the three resonances peak at about 31 °C (1544 nm), about 39 °C (1537 nm) and about 53 °C (1565 nm), each with a width of roughly 12 °C.
quotes: Temperature dependency of perfect phase matching for diﬀerent resonances.
assertions.certainty_reason: Values read by eye from the plot.

assertions.value: The authors estimate that a similarly phase-matched microring with a 15 µm radius would improve the SHG efficiency by over 5 times, because of the smaller cavity mode volume.
quotes: can be improved by over 5 times, simply because of the reduction in the cavity mode volume.
assertions.certainty_reason: An estimate; no 15 µm device was measured.

assertions.value: The authors estimate that critical coupling for the pump and a 15 µm radius could raise the internal nonlinear conversion efficiency by a further 10 times, given the current intrinsic Q.
quotes: can be further enhanced by 10 times via critical coupling scheme for
assertions.certainty_reason: An estimate; not demonstrated.

assertions.value: The authors report from simulation that about 75 percent of the SH light generated in the microring is lost, and that an additional wrap waveguide could improve out-coupling by two times.
quotes: about 75 percent of the generated SH light is lost in the microring.
This can be improved by two times through utilizing additional wrap waveguide17
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation-based estimate; the improvement is a proposal.

assertions.value: The authors state that the efficiency is limited by the transverse mode-overlap integral between the 1550 nm TM0 and 775 nm TM2 modes in the submicron waveguide, which they call a drawback of the modal phase matching scheme, and name quasi-phase matching by periodic poling as important future work.
quotes: limited by those integral terms which is the
between 1550-nm TM0 and 775-nm TM2 modes in the submicron waveguide
an inevitable drawback of our modal phase matching scheme despite obtaining a plausible conversion
quasi-phase matching by periodic poling3 will be an important immediate
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of their scheme and the proposed remedy.

assertions.value: The authors state that instability from dynamical thermal behaviour in LNOI microresonators must be carefully addressed, and that stable temperature control and electrical tuning or locking will be needed as Q approaches 105 or 107.
quotes: Instability of linear and nonlinear properties of microresonator structre on LNOI due to dynamical thermal behavior
along with delicate electrical tuning or locking mechanism on chip will be necessary.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit on their microring approach.

assertions.value: The authors state that the estimated Δd for the LNOI microring is 10 times larger than for an aluminum nitride microring, implying a more stringent phase matching condition at identical quality factor.
quotes: is 10 times larger than other comparable platform such as aluminum nitride microring
assertions.certainty_reason: A comparison with a cited value, stated without detail.

assertions.value: The authors cite prior work (Wang et al.) that demonstrated natural phase matching on X-cut LNOI with a normalized SHG efficiency of about 41%W−1cm−2, but restricted to one direction of light propagation.
quotes: ∼ 41%W −1cm−2 for second-harmonic generation (SHG).
the phase matching is restricted to only a particular direction of light propagation
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that they demonstrated modal-engineered natural phase matching in straight waveguides and microrings on monolithic Z-cut LNOI, with phase-matched SHG at 26%W−1cm−2 in the waveguide and a net 10 times efficiency enhancement in the microring.
quotes: we observe phase-matched SHG with 26%W −1cm−2
naturally phase matched SHG with a net enhancement of 10 times in
assertions.certainty_reason: Summary of the empirical results of one study.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 3(a): the measured phase-matching curve of the 1 mm waveguide has its main peak at about 1548 nm, with side peaks of about 0.6 at about 1543 nm and about 0.33 at about 1552 nm. Read from Figure 3(b): the SFG output falls from about 98.7 mV to about 96.7 mV.
quotes: Phase matching curve in IR band for the waveguide with L = 1 mm, top width
Sum frequency generation on the same waveguide.
assertions.certainty_reason: Values read by eye from the plot.
assertions.reader_inference: The dip of about 2 mV on about 98.7 mV is consistent with the 2% dip stated in the text.
